clinicalPearls: Compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root causes dermatomal arm pain, paraesthesiae, and sometimes myotomal weakness
The C6 and C7 roots are most commonly affected: C6 radiates to the thumb and C7 to the middle finger
The Spurling test (extension, ipsilateral rotation, and axial compression of the neck) reproduces radicular arm symptoms
The shoulder abduction relief sign, in which resting the arm on the head eases symptoms, supports a radicular cause
Reflex changes help localise the level: a reduced biceps or brachioradialis jerk suggests C6 and a reduced triceps jerk suggests C7
Most cases arise from either a soft disc herniation in younger patients or foraminal narrowing from spondylosis in older patients
The natural history is usually favourable, with most patients improving on conservative treatment (analgesia, physiotherapy, activity modification, nerve-root injection)
Progressive weakness, myelopathic signs, or failure of conservative care prompt MRI and consideration of foraminotomy, discectomy, or fusion
reference.pathophysiology: Cervical radiculopathy is dysfunction of a cervical nerve root caused by mechanical compression and chemical irritation. In younger patients a soft posterolateral disc herniation is the usual cause, whereas in older patients narrowing of the intervertebral foramen by uncovertebral and facet osteophytes (spondylosis) predominates. Compression together with accompanying inflammation of the root produces pain, sensory disturbance, and, in a myotomal distribution, motor weakness and reflex loss corresponding to the affected level.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy when long-tract signs are present
Peripheral nerve entrapment such as carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome
Brachial plexopathy or neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome)
Rotator cuff disease or other primary shoulder pathology
Pancoast tumour or other apical lesion
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the cervical spine for persistent or progressive symptoms
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to confirm the root level and exclude peripheral entrapment
Plain and oblique radiographs to assess foraminal narrowing and alignment
CT to characterise osteophytes when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated
Diagnostic selective nerve-root block to confirm the symptomatic level
redFlags: Signs of myelopathy such as gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, or hyperreflexia indicating cord compression
Constitutional features or a history of malignancy suggesting a neoplastic cause
reference.prognosis: Most patients with cervical radiculopathy improve within weeks to a few months with conservative measures, and surgery reliably relieves arm pain in those who fail conservative treatment or develop significant weakness.
pitfalls: Confusing radiculopathy with primary shoulder pathology or peripheral nerve entrapment
Missing coexisting myelopathy by not examining for long-tract signs
Operating for pain alone without a corroborating match between imaging and the clinical level
references: Bland: Disorders of the Cervical Spine
